To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) DAC, MAC, RBAC are all “special cases” of ABAC, (2) DAC, MAC and ABAC are “equivalent” in the sense of being “computationally equivalent” and (3) RBAC can be “implemented” in ABAC.
the ABAC models of [1, 2, 3] can be configured to be DAC, MAC, RBAC, or any combination of the three, and that the model of [4] can be configured only to be DAC or RBAC, but not MAC.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(1) defining a unified ABAC model, (2) defining a set of ABAC models that are “just sufficient” to cover DAC, MAC and the three variants of RBAC, and (3) establishing a set of “natural” mappings between these models.
a formal analysis and synthesis of the DAC, MAC and ABAC models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ABAC is not DAC, MAC, or RBAC, but that ABAC is a generalization of DAC, MAC, and RBAC.
ABAC is a model that is based on the attributes of subjects, objects and environment, and that is used to make access control decisions.
our model is a “unified ABAC model covering DAC, MAC and role based access control”.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed an attribute-based access control model that can be configured to do DAC and MAC with tranquility and hierarchical RBAC, while retaining the advantages of ABAC, such as flexibility, expressiveness, scalability, and simplicity.
we have developed a unified ABAC model that is capable of covering all of the features of DAC, MAC and flat and hierarchical RB AC.
we have shown that DAC, MAC and ABAC are not mutually exclusive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the three classical models are not as different as one might have thought.
ABAC models should have a lattice-based access control component and a role component, with the lattice component having a “transquility” property.
the three classical models are all instances of ABAC and the differences between the models are not fundamental.
